paper.title: The heterogeneous effects of education on crime: Evidence from Danish administrative twin data
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference is given. …

registers.role: sample frame / treatment / outcomes / controls / linkage

registers.name_in_paper: crime data (conviction data combined with data on charges)
registers.role: outcomes (adult conviction and incarceration ages 18-30) and controls (juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16); also the municipal youth conviction rate used to split neighbourhoods
treatment (completion of upper secondary education, specific qualifications, years of education) and, in Table A2, outcome; also parental education
sample frame and controls: unique personal identification number, sex, age, marital status, nationality, birth date (used to define twins), municipality of residence
linkage: children linked to parents by identification number, childhood household identification, parental education
described as part of Danish Register Data; no variable from it is used in a reported specification
described as part of Danish Register Data; no variable from it is used in a reported specification

registers.name_in_paper: data on the number of hospitalizations from ages 1-5
registers.role: controls: proxy for early childhood health in Table 8, columns (1) and (2)

linkages: Each individual has a unique identification number, which is used to match individuals across the various data sources.
Children are linked to parents using their identification numbers, which makes household characteristics during childhood and parental education available.
Twins are defined as individuals who are born on the same day and have both the same mother and father (no twin register or zygosity data is used).
Conviction data is combined with data on charges to recover the exact date the offense was committed.

Twins are linked to the municipality of residence in the year they are aged 14, and that municipality to its youth conviction rate (the fraction of individuals aged 15-25 convicted of a crime in a given year) relative to the median municipality.

sample.universe: All twins born 1965-1982 identified in Danish Register Data, i.e. all individuals born on the same day with both the same mother and father; the data covers every Danish resident 1980-2012.
sample.unit_of_observation: individual twin, nested in twin pairs (the within-twin-pair comparison is the estimating unit; standard errors are clustered at the twin pair / family level)
selection_rules: All twins born 1965-1982 (1965 is the first cohort for which juvenile crime from age 15 is observable; 1982 is the last cohort for which all crimes until age 30 can be followed).
Only twin pairs where both twins are continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012.
Twins who, at any point below the age of 15, were raised in different childhood households are excluded (280 twins in the final estimation sample have different childhood households).
Different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, are excluded; estimation is always split by gender of the twin pair.
Zygosity data is unavailable, so same-gender dizygotic twins remain in the final sample (which comprises an approximately equal amount of MZ and DZ twins).
For the parental education analysis, 698 same gender, same household twin pairs with missing parental education information are excluded.
For the early health analysis, the sample is restricted to the 1032 male twin pairs born 1976-1982 for whom hospitalization data at ages 1-5 exist.
For Table 6, the sample is further restricted to twin pairs where one twin has the exact qualification analysed and one twin does not.
For Table 8 columns (4)-(6), twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education are excluded, leaving 2399 male pairs.
For Fig. 1 the same-childhood-household restriction is not imposed for either the sibling or the twin samples.
sample.period: 1980-2012 (birth cohorts 1965-1982; crime measured over ages 18-30, juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16)
sample.n_observations: 5,696 male twin individuals (2,848 pairs) and 5,432 female twin individuals (2,716 pairs); 11,128 twins (5,564 pairs) in the summary statistics of Tables 1-3. Fig. 1 uses 516,238 in the 50% population sample, 476,392 in the sibling sample, 16,282 in the all twin sample and 11,408 in the same gender twin sample.
sample.n_individuals: 11,128 twins in the combined male and female twin sample

construction_notes: Crime is a binary variable indicating whether a twin was convicted of a crime as an adult, defined from the ages of 18 to 30; the upper age restriction makes crime observable over the same age ranges for all twins.

Total crimes follow the Danish classification of offenses: sexual, violent, property, narcotics, firearms, tax, unknown and other crimes, plus crimes against special legislation. Traffic violations, citations and accidents recorded in police data are excluded.
Types of offenses rather than specific offenses are used throughout, because detailed offenses contain too few observations once estimating within twins.

Education is primarily a binary variable equal to 1 if the individual attained a specific qualification as their highest completed education; the main measure is completion of (at least) upper secondary education. Education of 9 or 10 years is referred to as lower secondary education.
Years of education is imputed from the typical time it takes to attain a qualification, not observed schooling length.

Juvenile crime is captured by two separate indicators: convicted of a crime while aged 15, and while aged 16. The age of criminal responsibility in Denmark is 15, so crimes committed at age 14 or younger are unobservable.
Juvenile crime 15 or 16 (Table A2, columns 2 and 4) equals one if an individual is convicted of a juvenile crime at the age of 15 or 16.
Parental education is defined as high if a parent has been educated to the upper secondary level or beyond, and low if a parent is educated to a level less than upper secondary education.

A high crime municipality is one where the youth conviction rate (the fraction of individuals aged 15-25 convicted of a crime in a given year, following Damm and Dustmann, 2014) is higher than that of the median municipality in the year the twin is aged 14; there are 275 municipalities in the period.
Early health is proxied by the number of hospitalizations from ages 1-5 (and by an indicator for ever visiting hospital at ages 1-5); birth weight and APGAR scores are not available.
For the figures, the dependent variable of Eq. (1) is restricted to crimes committed in cumulative age ranges (18-19, 18-20, ..., 18-30), each point being a separate regression.
A linear probability model is used throughout to facilitate comparison of coefficients across specifications; standard errors are clustered at the twin pair (family) level.

claims.statement: Completing upper secondary education is associated with a 23.0 percentage point lower probability of conviction for any crime from ages 18-30 for male twins, in a cross-sectional OLS regression with birth cohort dummies and no juvenile crime controls.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), education data; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if an individual has attained (at least) upper secondary education as their highest completed education -- high school (regular academic, business or technical), vocational secondary education, or education beyond these two categories; 0 if educated only to lower secondary level (9 or 10 years).

timing.value: Highest completed educational qualification; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin has been convicted of a crime as an adult, defined from the ages of 18 to 30. Total crimes correspond to the Danish classification of offenses and comprise sexual, violent, property, narcotics, firearms, tax, unknown and other crimes, as well as crimes against special legislation; traffic violations, citations and accidents are excluded.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; the paper reports these as percentage points, so -0.095 is 9.5 percentage points), from a linear probability model

magnitude.interpretation: the completion of upper secondary education is associated with a reduction in the probability of conviction by 23 percentage points for males

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household; the paper presents these estimates as associations for that sample, not as causal effects.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30

population.description: Male same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: None: cross-sectional variation in educational attainment across individuals, with birth cohort dummy variables only. The paper presents these as associations and states they fail to deal with the endogenous relationship between education and crime.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional independence given birth cohort dummy variables (and, in even columns, juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16): the paper reports these OLS estimates as associations and states explicitly that they fail to deal with the endogenous relationship between education and crime.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper rejects this assumption and moves to within twin fixed effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author states this fails: unobservable characteristics which drive criminal activity and education bias the OLS estimates, so OLS may detect a negative relationship even if there is no causal effect of education on crime.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 and the comparison of Table 4 with the twin fixed effects estimates of Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: same-gender twin pairs, both twins continuously resident in Denmark 1980-2012 and raised in the same childhood household (for Table 4; the Fig. 1 sibling and twin samples do not impose the same-household restriction).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 comparison of twins with the sibling and 50% population samples.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; stated that little can be done to investigate this.

threats_discussed: Differences in unobservable factors (the classic example being ability) which affect both education and crime are determined by more than genetic factors (Bound and Solon, 1999; Griliches, 1979)
Zygosity is unobserved, so same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample and within-twin estimation produces biased results that likely overstate the crime-reducing effect of education
Early differences in health, potentially from birth (competition for nutrients in utero, birth weight), could drive differences in twin education levels
Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education
robustness_checks: Controlling for early health (number of hospital visits and ever visited hospital ages 1-5) for the 1032 male twin pairs born 1976-1982 (Table 8, columns 1-2)
Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence
unresolved_confounders: Remaining bias from same-gender DZ twins who cannot be excluded without zygosity data, so the results represent an upper bound on the crime reducing capabilities of education
Twins experience different environmental factors, particularly in school, so equality of unobservables (Ai1 = Ai2) may fail even for MZ twins
Measurement error if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection; no alternative measures such as self-reported crime are available
Whether the observed heterogeneity is due to parental education and exposure to youth crime themselves or to some other factor these measures capture

claims.statement: Completing upper secondary education is associated with a 14.0 percentage point lower probability of conviction for a property crime from ages 18-30 for male twins, controlling for juvenile crime.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), education data; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if an individual has attained (at least) upper secondary education as their highest completed education -- high school (regular academic, business or technical), vocational secondary education, or education beyond these two categories; 0 if educated only to lower secondary level (9 or 10 years).

timing.value: Highest completed educational qualification; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a property crime; property crimes comprise forgery, check forgery, arson, various degrees of burglary, theft from vehicles, theft of various vehicles, shoplifting, larceny, embezzlement, fraud, blackmail, robbery, handling stolen goods, tax evasion, malicious damage to property, and offenses against property.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; the paper reports these as percentage points, so -0.095 is 9.5 percentage points), from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household; the paper presents these estimates as associations for that sample, not as causal effects.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30

population.description: Male same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: None: cross-sectional variation in educational attainment across individuals, with birth cohort dummy variables only. The paper presents these as associations and states they fail to deal with the endogenous relationship between education and crime.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional independence given birth cohort dummy variables (and, in even columns, juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16): the paper reports these OLS estimates as associations and states explicitly that they fail to deal with the endogenous relationship between education and crime.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper rejects this assumption and moves to within twin fixed effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author states this fails: unobservable characteristics which drive criminal activity and education bias the OLS estimates, so OLS may detect a negative relationship even if there is no causal effect of education on crime.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 and the comparison of Table 4 with the twin fixed effects estimates of Table 5.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: same-gender twin pairs, both twins continuously resident in Denmark 1980-2012 and raised in the same childhood household (for Table 4; the Fig. 1 sibling and twin samples do not impose the same-household restriction).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 comparison of twins with the sibling and 50% population samples.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; stated that little can be done to investigate this.

threats_discussed: Differences in unobservable factors (the classic example being ability) which affect both education and crime are determined by more than genetic factors (Bound and Solon, 1999; Griliches, 1979)
Zygosity is unobserved, so same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample and within-twin estimation produces biased results that likely overstate the crime-reducing effect of education
Early differences in health, potentially from birth (competition for nutrients in utero, birth weight), could drive differences in twin education levels
Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education
robustness_checks: Controlling for early health (number of hospital visits and ever visited hospital ages 1-5) for the 1032 male twin pairs born 1976-1982 (Table 8, columns 1-2)
Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence
unresolved_confounders: Remaining bias from same-gender DZ twins who cannot be excluded without zygosity data, so the results represent an upper bound on the crime reducing capabilities of education
Twins experience different environmental factors, particularly in school, so equality of unobservables (Ai1 = Ai2) may fail even for MZ twins
Measurement error if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection; no alternative measures such as self-reported crime are available
Whether the observed heterogeneity is due to parental education and exposure to youth crime themselves or to some other factor these measures capture

Behavioral disorders affecting one twin

Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history

Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the individual was convicted of a crime while aged 16. Limiting the variable to crimes committed below the age of 17 is said to increase its plausible exogeneity because students are still bound by compulsory schooling laws.

timing.value: Conviction for a crime committed at age 16, i.e. before the adult (18-30) crime window and inside the compulsory-schooling window.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a property crime; property crimes comprise forgery, check forgery, arson, various degrees of burglary, theft from vehicles, theft of various vehicles, shoplifting, larceny, embezzlement, fraud, blackmail, robbery, handling stolen goods, tax evasion, malicious damage to property, and offenses against property.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; 0.257 is 25.7 percentage points), from a linear probability model

anchor_quote.text: Having committed crime as a juvenile is significantly and positively related to the probability of conviction across crime types for males, and less so for females.

claims.statement: Within male twin pairs, completing upper secondary education lowers the probability of conviction for total crime from ages 18-30 by 0.098 (twin fixed effects, without juvenile crime controls).

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), education data; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if an individual has attained (at least) upper secondary education as their highest completed education -- high school (regular academic, business or technical), vocational secondary education, or education beyond these two categories; 0 if educated only to lower secondary level (9 or 10 years).

timing.value: Highest completed educational qualification; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin has been convicted of a crime as an adult, defined from the ages of 18 to 30. Total crimes correspond to the Danish classification of offenses and comprise sexual, violent, property, narcotics, firearms, tax, unknown and other crimes, as well as crimes against special legislation; traffic violations, citations and accidents are excluded.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; the paper reports these as percentage points, so -0.095 is 9.5 percentage points), from a linear probability model

magnitude.interpretation: reduces an individual's probability of conviction of any crime by 9.8 percentage points (59% of the sample mean)

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twins born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household. The author argues that, unlike compulsory-schooling-reform designs, effects are identified over the entire population rather than only from compliers at the lower end of the educational distribution.
estimand.compliers: Identified only from twin pairs discordant in education: 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs differ in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs); 62% of all twin pairs differ when education is defined in years.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30
estimand.formal_query: E[C_ij | do(S_ij=1)] - E[C_ij | do(S_ij=0)] for same-gender twins raised in the same childhood household, conditional on the twin pair fixed effect alpha_i and the juvenile crime controls

population.description: Male same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if an individual has attained (at least) upper secondary education as their highest completed education -- high school (regular academic, business or technical), vocational secondary education, or education beyond these two categories; 0 if educated only to lower secondary level (9 or 10 years).

timing.value: Highest completed educational qualification; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a property crime; property crimes comprise forgery, check forgery, arson, various degrees of burglary, theft from vehicles, theft of various vehicles, shoplifting, larceny, embezzlement, fraud, blackmail, robbery, handling stolen goods, tax evasion, malicious damage to property, and offenses against property.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; the paper reports these as percentage points, so -0.095 is 9.5 percentage points), from a linear probability model

magnitude.interpretation: 8 percentage points, 76% of the sample mean (conclusion, p. 174)

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twins born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household. The author argues that, unlike compulsory-schooling-reform designs, effects are identified over the entire population rather than only from compliers at the lower end of the educational distribution.
estimand.compliers: Identified only from twin pairs discordant in education: 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs differ in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs); 62% of all twin pairs differ when education is defined in years.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30
estimand.formal_query: E[C_ij | do(S_ij=1)] - E[C_ij | do(S_ij=0)] for same-gender twins raised in the same childhood household, conditional on the twin pair fixed effect alpha_i and the juvenile crime controls

population.description: Male same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16 is a plausibly exogenous proxy control: because these crimes fall inside the compulsory schooling window, juvenile crime is less likely to directly affect an individual's educational attainment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from compulsory schooling laws; the paper also acknowledges the exogeneity of the dummy is uncertain, reports every baseline result with and without the control, and directly estimates the effect of juvenile convictions on education in Table A2.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper states that alternative measures such as self-reported crime are unavailable and little can be done to investigate the issue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sufficient within-twin-pair variation in education exists in the estimation sample and in each subsample analysed, so that the within-twin comparison is identified off discordant pairs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs with within-pair variation in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs), and 62% of all twins when education is defined in years; Table A1 reports the same for each subsample.

threats_discussed: Differences in unobservable factors (the classic example being ability) which affect both education and crime are determined by more than genetic factors (Bound and Solon, 1999; Griliches, 1979)
Zygosity is unobserved, so same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample and within-twin estimation produces biased results that likely overstate the crime-reducing effect of education
Early differences in health, potentially from birth (competition for nutrients in utero, birth weight), could drive differences in twin education levels
Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education
robustness_checks: Controlling for early health (number of hospital visits and ever visited hospital ages 1-5) for the 1032 male twin pairs born 1976-1982 (Table 8, columns 1-2)
Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence
unresolved_confounders: Remaining bias from same-gender DZ twins who cannot be excluded without zygosity data, so the results represent an upper bound on the crime reducing capabilities of education
Twins experience different environmental factors, particularly in school, so equality of unobservables (Ai1 = Ai2) may fail even for MZ twins
Measurement error if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection; no alternative measures such as self-reported crime are available
Whether the observed heterogeneity is due to parental education and exposure to youth crime themselves or to some other factor these measures capture

population.description: Female same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16 is a plausibly exogenous proxy control: because these crimes fall inside the compulsory schooling window, juvenile crime is less likely to directly affect an individual's educational attainment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from compulsory schooling laws; the paper also acknowledges the exogeneity of the dummy is uncertain, reports every baseline result with and without the control, and directly estimates the effect of juvenile convictions on education in Table A2.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper states that alternative measures such as self-reported crime are unavailable and little can be done to investigate the issue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sufficient within-twin-pair variation in education exists in the estimation sample and in each subsample analysed, so that the within-twin comparison is identified off discordant pairs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs with within-pair variation in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs), and 62% of all twins when education is defined in years; Table A1 reports the same for each subsample.

Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education

Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence
unresolved_confounders: Remaining bias from same-gender DZ twins who cannot be excluded without zygosity data, so the results represent an upper bound on the crime reducing capabilities of education

anchor_quote.text: For female twins, completing upper secondary education has a negative and significant impact on total crimes, with less significant impacts on property and violent crimes.

claims.statement: Within female twin pairs, completing upper secondary education lowers the probability of conviction for violent crime from ages 18-30 by 0.005 (twin fixed effects, without juvenile crime controls).

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), education data; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if an individual has attained (at least) upper secondary education as their highest completed education -- high school (regular academic, business or technical), vocational secondary education, or education beyond these two categories; 0 if educated only to lower secondary level (9 or 10 years).

timing.value: Highest completed educational qualification; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a violent crime; violent crimes comprise violence against public authorities, disturbance of public order, homicide, attempted homicide, varying degrees of assault, intentional bodily harm, offenses against life, and threats.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; the paper reports these as percentage points, so -0.095 is 9.5 percentage points), from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twins born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household. subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.

timing.value: Highest completed qualification converted to years; the paper does not state the calendar year or age at which attainment is measured.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a property crime; property crimes comprise forgery, check forgery, arson, various degrees of burglary, theft from vehicles, theft of various vehicles, shoplifting, larceny, embezzlement, fraud, blackmail, robbery, handling stolen goods, tax evasion, malicious damage to property, and offenses against property.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 per additional year of education (a proportion; the paper reports -0.017 as 1.7 percentage points), from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twins born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household. The author argues that, unlike compulsory-schooling-reform designs, effects are identified over the entire population rather than only from compliers at the lower end of the educational distribution.
estimand.compliers: Identified only from twin pairs discordant in education: 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs differ in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs); 62% of all twin pairs differ when education is defined in years.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30
estimand.formal_query: E[C_ij | do(S_ij=1)] - E[C_ij | do(S_ij=0)] for same-gender twins raised in the same childhood household, conditional on the twin pair fixed effect alpha_i and the juvenile crime controls

population.description: Female same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16 is a plausibly exogenous proxy control: because these crimes fall inside the compulsory schooling window, juvenile crime is less likely to directly affect an individual's educational attainment.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from compulsory schooling laws; the paper also acknowledges the exogeneity of the dummy is uncertain, reports every baseline result with and without the control, and directly estimates the effect of juvenile convictions on education in Table A2.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper states that alternative measures such as self-reported crime are unavailable and little can be done to investigate the issue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sufficient within-twin-pair variation in education exists in the estimation sample and in each subsample analysed, so that the within-twin comparison is identified off discordant pairs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs with within-pair variation in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs), and 62% of all twins when education is defined in years; Table A1 reports the same for each subsample.

Early differences in health, potentially from birth (competition for nutrients in utero, birth weight), could drive differences in twin education levels
Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education

Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence

population.description: Male same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Within-twin-pair variation in juvenile crime convictions at ages 15-16 is exogenous to educational attainment conditional on the twin pair fixed effect; the paper notes that including a juvenile crime variable can be read as a lagged dependent variable, which under within twin fixed effects would produce biased results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test; the paper flags the concern in a footnote and in the discussion of whether a juvenile crime dummy can be considered truly exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper states that alternative measures such as self-reported crime are unavailable and little can be done to investigate the issue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sufficient within-twin-pair variation in education exists in the estimation sample and in each subsample analysed, so that the within-twin comparison is identified off discordant pairs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs with within-pair variation in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs), and 62% of all twins when education is defined in years; Table A1 reports the same for each subsample.

Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the individual was convicted of a crime while aged 15. Limiting the variable to crimes committed below the age of 17 is said to increase its plausible exogeneity because students are still bound by compulsory schooling laws.

timing.value: Conviction for a crime committed at age 15, i.e. before the adult (18-30) crime window and inside the compulsory-schooling window.

register_source.value: Danish Register Data (Statistics Denmark), crime data: conviction data combined with data on charges to use the exact date the offense was committed; no DST register code or variable name is given in the paper

definition.value: Binary variable equal to 1 if the twin was convicted from ages 18-30 of a property crime; property crimes comprise forgery, check forgery, arson, various degrees of burglary, theft from vehicles, theft of various vehicles, shoplifting, larceny, embezzlement, fraud, blackmail, robbery, handling stolen goods, tax evasion, malicious damage to property, and offenses against property.

timing.value: Convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30; a single cumulative indicator over that age window, imposed so that crime is observable over the same age ranges for all twins

units.value: change in the probability of conviction from ages 18-30 (a proportion; 0.101 is 10.1 percentage points), from a linear probability model

estimand.target_population: Danish same-gender twins born 1965-1982 raised in the same childhood household. The author argues that, unlike compulsory-schooling-reform designs, effects are identified over the entire population rather than only from compliers at the lower end of the educational distribution.
estimand.compliers: Identified only from the 2.2% (age 15) and 2.7% (age 16) of twin pairs with different juvenile crime outcomes reported in Table 3.
estimand.time_horizon: convictions for crimes committed from the ages of 18 to 30
estimand.formal_query: E[C_ij | do(S_ij=1)] - E[C_ij | do(S_ij=0)] for same-gender twins raised in the same childhood household, conditional on the twin pair fixed effect alpha_i and the juvenile crime controls

population.description: Female same-gender twin pairs born 1965-1982, with both twins continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or from birth for those born after 1980) to 2012, and raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
population.ages: crime outcome measured over ages 18-30; juvenile crime at ages 15 and 16
subgroups_defined: at least one parent with low education vs both parents with high education
high vs low youth-crime municipality of residence at age 14
educational program (any high school / university / vocational)
population.selection: Twin pairs where both twins were continuously in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012; twin pairs raised in different childhood households below age 15 excluded (280 twins); different-gendered twin pairs, approximately 30% of twins, excluded; zygosity unobserved so same-gender DZ twins remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Differences in educational attainment within same-gender twin pairs raised in the same childhood household; the twin pair fixed effect absorbs genetic, environmental and familial factors common to the two twins.

key_assumptions.assumption: Equality of unobservables within twin pairs: unobservable factors are constant across twins (Ai1 = Ai2), so that conditional on the twin pair fixed effect and the included controls, differences in educational attainment within a twin pair are exogenous.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from twins being genetically similar and usually raised in the same environment; supported indirectly by excluding twins raised in different childhood households, by excluding different-gendered (necessarily DZ) twins, and by Fig. 1 showing the same-gender twin fixed-effects estimate is the smallest in absolute magnitude of all family fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: The author concedes this assumption fails in part: lacking data on zygosity, same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample, so unobservable characteristics which differ between twins drive both crime and education decisions and within twin estimation produces biased results that overstate the crime reducing effect of education.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Zygosity shares from Skytthe et al. (2011); Bound and Solon (1999) and Griliches (1979) critique; Fig. 1 comparison of OLS, sibling and twin fixed-effects estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Within-twin-pair variation in juvenile crime convictions at ages 15-16 is exogenous to educational attainment conditional on the twin pair fixed effect; the paper notes that including a juvenile crime variable can be read as a lagged dependent variable, which under within twin fixed effects would produce biased results.
key_assumptions.supported_by: No direct test; the paper flags the concern in a footnote and in the discussion of whether a juvenile crime dummy can be considered truly exogenous.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: the estimation sample is conditioned on being a same-gender twin pair, on both twins being continuously resident in Denmark from 1980 (or birth) to 2012, and on both twins being raised in the same childhood household at every point below age 15.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 1 compares OLS estimates across a 50% population sample, the sibling population and the twin population to argue twins are relatively similar to the overall population.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference between twins beyond what the juvenile crime controls absorb: peer effects whereby the crime of one twin encourages or discourages the adult crime of the other twin are assumed to be taken into account by controlling for the juvenile crime of one twin.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in a footnote; no test is reported.

key_assumptions.assumption: Crime is measured without differential error: individuals are only classified as criminals if they are apprehended, and the paper states that if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates will be biased.
key_assumptions.supported_by: None; the paper states that alternative measures such as self-reported crime are unavailable and little can be done to investigate the issue.

key_assumptions.assumption: Sufficient within-twin-pair variation in education exists in the estimation sample and in each subsample analysed, so that the within-twin comparison is identified off discordant pairs.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 3 reports 17.8% of male and 14.4% of female twin pairs with within-pair variation in completion of upper secondary education (more than 500 male and 390 female pairs), and 62% of all twins when education is defined in years; Table A1 reports the same for each subsample.

Zygosity is unobserved, so same-gender DZ twins remain in the sample and within-twin estimation produces biased results that likely overstate the crime-reducing effect of education
Early differences in health, potentially from birth (competition for nutrients in utero, birth weight), could drive differences in twin education levels
Congenital birth defects affecting one twin
Behavioral disorders affecting one twin
Reverse causality: participation in crime as a juvenile can directly affect educational attainment
The juvenile-crime control could be interpreted as a lagged dependent variable, which under within-twin fixed effects would produce biased results
Peer effects between twins (the crime of one twin encouraging or discouraging the other)
Twins raised in different childhood households experience vastly different environmental factors

Measurement error in crime data, since individuals are only classified as criminals if apprehended; if more skilled criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection the estimates are biased
Outlying twin pairs with large differences in education
robustness_checks: Controlling for early health (number of hospital visits and ever visited hospital ages 1-5) for the 1032 male twin pairs born 1976-1982 (Table 8, columns 1-2)
Using conviction to a prison term instead of any conviction as the dependent variable (Table 8, column 3)
Excluding male twin pairs with 4 or more years difference in education (Table 8, columns 4-6)
Directly estimating the reverse causality of juvenile convictions on completing upper secondary education (Table A2)
Comparing OLS and family fixed effects estimates across a 50% population sample, siblings, all twins and same-gender twins (Fig. 1)
Reporting every baseline specification with and without controls for juvenile crime history
Logit regression with twin fixed effects (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Defining crime as the number of convictions from ages 18-30 instead of the probability of conviction (unreported, stated to give similar results)
Specifications excluding juvenile crime at age 16
Alternative age ranges for the early-health hospitalization proxy, including from age 0
Alternative ages for measuring municipality of residence
unresolved_confounders: Remaining bias from same-gender DZ twins who cannot be excluded without zygosity data, so the results represent an upper bound on the crime reducing capabilities of education
Twins experience different environmental factors, particularly in school, so equality of unobservables (Ai1 = Ai2) may fail even for MZ twins
Measurement error if more skilled or clever criminals are both more educated and better able to avoid detection; no alternative measures such as self-reported crime are available
Whether the observed heterogeneity is due to parental education and exposure to youth crime themselves or to some other factor these measures capture
